# From probabilities to actions {#sec-ch04}

::: {.epigraph by="William Bruce Cameron, Informal Sociology, 1963"}
Not everything that can be counted counts, and not everything that counts can be counted.
:::

You now have probabilities you can trust: when the model says 20%, about one in five of those alerts is an attack. Next comes the question everyone reaches: *where do I put the threshold?*

Most people pick 0.5. It's the default in almost every library, and it *feels* neutral. It isn't. It's a very specific opinion about your business, usually the wrong one. This chapter puts the threshold where it belongs, with school arithmetic.

::: {.goals}
- Turn two costs into one threshold, and explain why 0.5 is a special case.
- See why the formula only works when the probabilities are calibrated.
- Read the precision–recall trade-off as a business choice.
- Treat "I don't know, ask a person" as a real action, and meet the three doors: act, review, escalate.
:::

## The umbrella question

The forecast says 30% chance of rain. Do you take an umbrella? It depends on two things you already know. Carrying an umbrella you didn't need is a little annoying; call it 1 unit of annoyance. Getting very wet on the way to a meeting is much worse; call it 4.

If you carry it, you pay 1, rain or not. If you leave it, you pay 4, but only if it rains. So on average you pay 4 × the chance of rain.

![The umbrella decision. Carrying always costs 1. Leaving it costs 4 times the chance of rain. The lines cross at 20%: above that, carry it.](/figures/ch05/umbrella.pdf){#fig-umbrella}

The two lines in @fig-umbrella cross where 4 × *P* = 1, which is *P* = 0.2. Above a 20% chance of rain, carry the umbrella. Below it, leave it at home. At 30%, you take it, even though it probably won't rain.

Everything else in this chapter is that umbrella, applied to real work.

## One formula, two costs

Replace the umbrella with any yes-or-no action. There are two ways to get it wrong:

- a **false alarm**: you act, and you didn't need to (you carried the umbrella; you blocked a harmless login);
- a **miss**: you don't act, and you should have (you got wet; you let an attacker in).

If a false alarm costs *C*~fa~ and a miss costs *C*~miss~, the cheapest thing to do, on average, is this:

::: {.keyidea}
Act when P > C~fa~ ÷ (C~fa~ + C~miss~): the false-alarm cost over the sum of both costs.
:::

Check it with the umbrella: 1 ÷ (1 + 4) = 0.2. That's exactly where the two lines crossed.

When the two costs are equal, the formula gives 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. *That's* where 0.5 comes from: it's right only when a false alarm and a miss hurt exactly the same. That's almost never true of anything worth building a model for.

::: {.keyidea}
0.5 is not neutral: it's the threshold for a world where every mistake costs the same.
:::

![The right threshold for any ratio between the cost of a miss and the cost of a false alarm (both axes on a log scale). Equal costs give 0.5. As misses get more expensive, the threshold drops fast.](/figures/ch05/threshold-ratio.pdf){#fig-threshold-ratio}

@fig-threshold-ratio puts real decisions on one curve. Letting an alert close itself with nobody looking (Chapter 14) sits in the far corner: a miss is about 630 times worse than twelve minutes of a person's time, so the threshold falls to about {{< num ch05 soc_review_t f4 >}}. Different costs, different threshold.

::: {.deeper}
Where the formula comes from. For a single case with probability *P*, acting costs (1 − *P*) × *C*~fa~ on average, because you pay only if it was harmless. Not acting costs *P* × *C*~miss~, because you pay only if it was real. Act when the first is smaller: (1 − *P*) *C*~fa~ < *P* *C*~miss~. Rearranged, that's *P* > *C*~fa~ / (*C*~fa~ + *C*~miss~). Getting it *right* can also have costs or benefits; for example, blocking a real threat might earn some credit. Then the same logic works with a 2×2 table of costs, one for each combination of action and truth. This is the basis of cost-sensitive learning [@elkan2001].
:::

## Does it work on real alerts?

Test it. For every alert the team decides: **block it or allow it?** Wrongly blocking something harmless costs about \$200 in lost work (a delayed shipment, a locked-out engineer). Letting a real threat through costs about \$4,000, since other defences may still catch it. (Illustrative but realistic numbers.)

The formula says block when *P* > 200 ÷ 4,200, about {{< num ch05 t_formula f3 >}}. A brute-force search over 300 thresholds lands almost exactly there. Using 0.5 instead costs {{< num ch05 half_penalty f1 >}} times as much.

![Total cost on the test alerts at every threshold. For the calibrated model (green, solid line), the formula's threshold is near the lowest point of the curve. For the same model trained on rebalanced data (red, dashed line), the same threshold lands far from its lowest point.](/figures/ch05/cost-curve.pdf){#fig-cost-curve}

Now you see why calibration came first. The rebalanced model from Chapter 3 ranks almost as well, but its numbers are too high. Apply the formula to *its* numbers and the cost is {{< num ch05 bal_penalty pct >}} higher (@fig-cost-curve). Its own best threshold is far away, near {{< num ch05 t_bal_best f2 >}}, and only trial and error could find it, again every time the costs change.

::: {.keyidea}
With calibrated probabilities, costs set the threshold directly. Without them, you're guessing.
:::

Calibration turns threshold-setting from endless trial and error into one line of arithmetic you can explain to your finance team.

## Precision, recall, and the price of each

Precision and recall aren't two scores; they're two sides of one trade-off.

![As the threshold moves up, precision (how many blocks were real) rises and recall (how many threats got blocked) falls. The grey dotted curve shows how much traffic you're blocking. The vertical line is the cost-based threshold.](/figures/ch05/pr-threshold.pdf){#fig-pr-threshold}

At the cost-based threshold in @fig-pr-threshold, the team blocks about {{< num ch05 blocked_frac pct >}} of alerts. That catches {{< num ch05 caught pct >}} of real threats, but only {{< num ch05 precision pct >}} of the blocks are real ones. That precision sounds poor. Is it?

Only the costs can say. The rule blocks anything better than about 1 in 21 to be real, because a miss costs 20 times a false alarm. Precision, around one in five, is just the average over everything above that line. Nobody chose it; it falls out of the costs. A better-ranking model raises precision without moving the threshold at all. Precision or recall alone, without costs, is half a story.

::: {.threshold}
The sales team complains that blocked customer emails are losing them sales. They say a wrong block costs \$800, not \$200. Work out the blocking threshold again. About what happens to the share of alerts blocked, and to recall?

(800 ÷ 4,800 ≈ 0.17. The threshold moves up, fewer alerts get blocked, and more threats get through. The model didn't change. The business's priorities did, and the threshold should follow them.)
:::

## "I don't know" is an action too

There's almost always a third option, and it's the most useful: *don't decide; ask a person*. In 1970 the engineer C. K. Chow showed that a character-reading machine allowed to refuse its least certain cases made far fewer errors [@chow1970]. Today it's called *selective prediction* [@geifman2017].

Sort alerts by how sure the model is. Let the machine decide only the top of the list; send the rest to people.

![Coverage against risk. Reading from right to left: if the machine decides every alert, you take its full error rate. Let it decide only the alerts it's surest about and send the rest to people, and the error rate among its decisions falls steeply. A better model (green, solid line) gives you more coverage at the same risk.](/figures/ch05/coverage-risk.pdf){#fig-coverage-risk}

Deciding every alert, the model gets {{< num ch05 risk_100 pct1 >}} wrong. Deciding only the surest 80%, just {{< num ch05 risk_80 pct1 >}} of its decisions are wrong. Deciding the surest half, only {{< num ch05 risk_50 pct1 >}} are wrong.

::: {.keyidea}
Let a model decide only the cases it's surest about, and its error rate falls steeply.
:::

@fig-coverage-risk is one of the most useful pictures you can show a manager. It replaces "how good is the model?" with the question they actually have: *how much of this work can we safely hand over, at what error rate?*

## Three doors

Put the two ideas together, cost-based thresholds and "ask a person", and you get a design we'll use for the rest of the book.

![The three doors. At one end the model is confident nothing's needed, so the machine handles it. At the other end it's confident something's badly wrong, so a person is called in immediately. In between, where it's unsure, a person looks when they can.](/figures/ch05/three-doors.pdf){#fig-three-doors}

**Act** when the model is confident the machine can handle it alone. **Review** when it's unsure, so a person checks it as part of normal work. **Escalate** when it's confident something important is wrong, so a person is called in right now. These three choices are the book's three zones: act, review and escalate.

The two boundaries come from the same cost arithmetic, one threshold per action. Chapter 14 sets them, and handles the part skipped here: what happens when there aren't enough people for the middle zone.

::: {.breaks}
Costs are guesses, and the formula treats guesses like facts. Two habits help. Try each cost at half and at double, and see how far the threshold moves; if it barely moves, stop arguing about the exact number. And remember costs differ by case: a false alarm on the CEO's laptop costs more than on a test server. Some costs aren't money at all (trust, fairness, safety, law). Discuss them openly, or someone's default settings decide them for you.
:::

That's Part I. A machine asked for yes-or-no was useless, so we asked for a chance; learned what a chance means and how to check it; and let costs, not habit, place the thresholds, with a door left open for the cases a machine shouldn't decide alone. Every system in the rest of the book, from neural networks to LLMs to Jev, is judged by these four chapters.

::: {.exercises}
1. A hospital test flags a serious but treatable condition. Treating someone who doesn't have it costs \$500 and some discomfort; missing someone who does costs \$50,000. What's the treatment threshold? What would you want to know about the test's calibration before trusting it?
2. Explain in two sentences why "0.5 is the neutral threshold" is wrong.
3. Using @fig-coverage-risk, how much of the blocking decision could you automate if the business accepts a 2% error rate? Where would the rest go?
:::
